anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and bloating on-disk structures.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The generation, flushing, switching, or archiving of write-ahead log records becomes the bottleneck on the commit path, inflating commit latency and log storage.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated, so read/write latency, queue depths, and IOPS limits are exceeded across data, temp, and log volumes.

When these three root causes occur together, the database exhibits a compound symptom pattern: 1) rapidly expanding tables, indexes, version store, and transaction-log directories; 2) soaring commit and checkpoint latency dominated by log-flush and device-I/O waits; 3) long-running queries and autovacuum/clean-up workers that never catch up; 4) device-level queues pegged, with wait profiles simultaneously showing MVCC visibility checks, log-related waits, and generic data-file I/O stalls; 5) escalating risk of transaction-ID or log-segment wraparound, emergency checkpoints, and sudden write stalls that block both OLTP traffic and background maintenance.

Causally, high update/delete churn inflates the version store, which in turn increases redo generation because every version change must be logged; this heavier log stream stresses the transaction-log subsystem. Frequent log flushes and larger log archives multiply write pressure on the same storage back-end that is already servicing bloated data-file writes and long sequential scans caused by MVCC bloat. As the storage layer saturates, log flush latency rises, stretching transaction completion times and prolonging snapshot retention; the longer snapshots further delay version reclamation, feeding back into MVCC bloat. The intertwined feedback loops—more versions ⇒ more log writes ⇒ more physical I/O ⇒ slower cleanup ⇒ even more versions—can rapidly degrade throughput and threaten database availability.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
